chapter: Washington in the 1930s: big bands, lessons, first jobs
title: Jack Smith's one and only lesson
summary: His father hires Jack Smith as teacher, then dismisses him on the spot because he arrived drunk and taught without music.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: So, if I can digress a little bit, oh, about six or seven months after my uncle and my father brought this piano to the house, I had been coming in every evening, sitting and playing, and no one ever had to tell me to practice or anything like that. So they just let me play as much as I wanted to. And my mother was always very encouraging. And my father decided he would give me piano lessons. Well, there was a fellow, one of the friends of my father that used to come around, and he would play for little get-togethers that he would have at the house with the people from the various committees, the church or whatever, and he would have this friend... This fellow's name was Jack Smith. I never did know what happened to Jack Smith, but he was always what I thought of as a very good pianist. Anyway, I used to love to listen
to him, too. But my father decided that he would have Jack give me some piano lessons.

So when he told me about it, he said, "Mr. Smith is going to come by and give you some piano lessons, and he says he'll be by on Tuesday" or something. I could hardly wait, because this guy...to come and push this magic button and make me a pianist. But when he came in, I was sitting at the piano, I had been sitting at the piano for the last hour... He came in and he listened to a few little things I did, and then he sat down and played a couple of pieces. I was admiring him, and he said, "Oh, you liked that?" I said, "Yeah." So he said, "Okay, come on and sit down." And I sat down at the piano, and he learned over my shoulder and said, "Put your hand here and put your hand here, and put this finger here..."

As he was doing this, he was showing me these things on the keyboard, my father came in -- I guess a half-hour or an hour later, while he was doing it. And my father stopped him and asked to speak to him for a minute. And my father took him sort of over in the corner, and I heard them talking, and kind of in low tones. What I heard my father say was... He told this fellow Jack, "I don't ever want you ever to come back here like that again, and I don't want him taught like that." He was referring to me.
So the next thing I knew, Jack had his coat and hat and

was leaving. I was a little puzzled, but I don't... I didn't ask them for what reasons... I don't know why I didn't ask. But I learned later, because I think I communicated with my mother much better than I did my father, that what had happened... The reason for it was that Jack, when he came in, he had been drinking. Just how drunk he was I couldn't have surmised, because he wasn't staggering or anything. But my father must have known that he was pretty drunk. And this smell he had on his breath was the kind he always had, so I never knew the difference!
